Adiabatic Decoupling and Time-Dependent Born-Oppenheimer Theory

Herbert Spohn Affiliation: Zentrum Mathematik and Physik Department, Affiliation: Technische Universität München,    Stefan Teufel Affiliation: 80290 München, Germany Affiliation: email: spohn@ma.tum.de, teufel@ma.tum.de
July 9, 2001
Abstract

We reconsider the time-dependent Born-Oppenheimer theory with the goal to carefully separate between the adiabatic decoupling of a given group of energy bands from their orthogonal subspace and the semiclassics within the energy bands. Band crossings are allowed and our results are local in the sense that they hold up to the first time when a band crossing is encountered. The adiabatic decoupling leads to an effective Schrödinger equation for the nuclei, including contributions from the Berry connection.

1 Introduction

Molecules consist of light electrons, mass mem_{\rm e}, and heavy nuclei, mass MM which depends on the type of nucleus. Born and Oppenheimer [3] wanted to explain some general features of molecular spectra and realized that, since the ratio me/Mm_{\rm e}/M is small, it could be used as an expansion parameter for the energy levels of the molecular Hamiltonian. The time-independent Born-Oppenheimer theory has been put on firm mathematical grounds by Combes, Duclos, and Seiler [5], Hagedorn [8], and more recently in [16].

With the development of tailored state preparation and ultra precise time resolution there is a growing interest in understanding and controlling the dynamics of molecules, which requires an analysis of the solutions to the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, again exploiting that me/Mm_{\rm e}/M is small. The molecular Hamiltonian is of the form

H=ℏ22​me​(−i​∇x−Aext​(x))2+ℏ22​M​(−i​∇X+Aext​(X))2+Ve​(x)+Ven​(X,x)+Vn​(X).H=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m_{\rm e}}\Big(-i\nabla_{x}-A_{\rm ext}(x)\Big)^{2}+\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2M}\Big(-i\nabla_{X}+A_{\rm ext}(X)\Big)^{2}+V_{\rm e}(x)+V_{\rm en}(X,x)+V_{\rm n}(X)\,. (1)

For notational simplicity we ignore spin degrees of freedom and assume that all nuclei have the same mass. We have kk electrons with positions {x1,…,xk}=x\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\}=x and ll nuclei with positions {X1,…,Xl}=X\{X_{1},\ldots,X_{l}\}=X. The first and second term of HH are the kinetic energies of the electrons and of the nuclei, respectively. An external magnetic field is included through the vector potential AextA_{\rm ext}. Electrons and nuclei interact via the static Coulomb potential. Therefore VeV_{\rm e} is the electronic, VnV_{\rm n} the nucleonic repulsion, and VenV_{\rm en} the attraction between electrons and nuclei. VeV_{\rm e} and VnV_{\rm n} may also contain an external electrostatic potential.

In atomic units (me=ℏ=1m_{\rm e}=\hbar=1) the Hamiltonian (1) can be written more concisely as

H=meM​12​(−i​∇X+Aext​(X))2+He​(X),H=\,\frac{m_{\rm e}}{M}\,\frac{1}{2}\Big(-i\nabla_{X}+A_{\rm ext}(X)\Big)^{2}+H_{\rm e}(X)\,, (2)

emphasizing that the nuclear kinetic energy will be treated as a “small perturbation”. He​(X)H_{\rm e}(X) is the electronic Hamiltonian for given position XX of the nuclei,

He​(X)=12​(−i​∇x−Aext​(x))2+Ve​(x)+Ven​(X,x)+Vn​(X).H_{\rm e}(X)=\frac{1}{2}\Big(-i\nabla_{x}-A_{\rm ext}(x)\Big)^{2}+V_{\rm e}(x)+V_{\rm en}(X,x)+V_{\rm n}(X)\,. (3)

He​(X)H_{\rm e}(X) is a self-adjoint operator on the electronic Hilbert space L2​(ℝ3​k)L^{2}({\mathbb{R}}^{3k}) restricted to its antisymmetric subspace. Later on we will need some smoothness of He​(X)H_{\rm e}(X), which can be established easily if the electrons are treated as point-like and the nuclei have an extended, rigid charge distribution.

Generically He​(X)H_{\rm e}(X) has, possibly degenerate, eigenvalues E1​(X)<E2​(X)<…E_{1}(X)<E_{2}(X)<\ldots which terminate at the continuum edge Σ⁡(X)\Sigma(X). Thereby one obtains the band structure as plotted schematically in Figure 1. The discrete bands Ej​(X)E_{j}(X) may cross and possibly merge into the continuous spectrum as indicated in Figure 2.

Comparing kinetic energies, we find for the speeds |vn|≈(me/M)1/2​|ve||v_{\rm n}|\approx(m_{\rm e}/M)^{1/2}|v_{\rm e}|, which means that on the atomic scale the nuclei move very slowly. If we regard X⁡(t)X(t) as a given nucleonic trajectory, then He​(X​(t))H_{\rm e}(X(t)) is a Hamiltonian with slow time variation and the time-adiabatic theorem [15, 14, 1] can be applied [2]. For us XX are quantum mechanical degrees of freedom. The Hamiltonian HH of (2) is time-independent and we can only exploit that the nucleonic Laplacian carries a small prefactor. To distinguish, we refer to our situation as space-adiabatic. Since the nuclei move very slowly, their dynamics must be followed over sufficiently long times. From the speed ratio we conclude that these times are of order (me/M)1/2(m_{\rm e}/M)^{1/2} in atomic units. To simplify notation we define

ε=meM\varepsilon=\sqrt{\frac{m_{\rm e}}{M}} (4)

as the small dimensionless parameter. Then

Hε=ε2​12​(−i​∇X+Aext​(X))2+He​(X),H^{\varepsilon}=\varepsilon^{2}\frac{1}{2}\Big(-i\nabla_{X}+A_{\rm ext}(X)\Big)^{2}+H_{\rm e}(X)\,, (5)

and we want to study the solutions of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation

i​ε​∂ψ∂t=Hε​ψi\varepsilon\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial t}=H^{\varepsilon}\psi (6)

in the limit of small ε\varepsilon.

The crude physical picture underlying the analysis of (6) is that the nuclei behave semiclassically because of their large mass and that the electrons rapidly adjust to the slow nucleonic motion. Thus, in fact, the time-dependent Born-Oppenheimer approximation involves two limits. If the electrons are initially in the eigenstate χj​(X0)\chi_{j}(X_{0}) of the jj-th band with energy Ej​(X0)E_{j}(X_{0}), where X0X_{0} is the approximate initial configuration of the nuclei, then the jj-th band is adiabatically protected provided there is an energy gap separating it from the rest of the spectrum. Thus at later times, up to small error, the electronic wave function is still in the subspace corresponding to the jj-th band. But this implies that the nuclei are governed by the Born-Oppenheimer Hamiltonian

HBOε=ε2​12​(−i​∇X+Aext​(X))2+Ej​(X).H^{\varepsilon}_{\rm BO}=\varepsilon^{2}\frac{1}{2}\Big(-i\nabla_{X}+A_{\rm ext}(X)\Big)^{2}+E_{j}(X)\,. (7)

Since ε≪1\varepsilon\ll 1, HBOεH_{\rm BO}^{\varepsilon} can be analyzed through semiclassical methods where to leading order the contributions come from the classical flow Φt\Phi^{t} corresponding to the classical Hamiltonian HBOcl=12​p2+Ej​(q)H_{\rm BO}^{\rm cl}=\frac{1}{2}p^{2}+E_{j}(q) on nucleonic phase space.

In general, Ej​(X)E_{j}(X) may touch another band as XX varies. To allow for such band crossings we introduce the region Λ⊂ℝn\Lambda\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n}, n=3​ln=3l, in nucleonic configuration space, such that EjE_{j} restricted to Λ\Lambda does not cross or touch any other energy band. The classical flow Φt\Phi^{t} then has Λ×ℝn\Lambda\times{\mathbb{R}}^{n} as phase space and is defined only up to the time when it first hits the boundary ∂Λ×ℝn\partial\Lambda\times{\mathbb{R}}^{n}. Up to that time (7) still correctly describes the quantum evolution. To follow the tunneling through a band crossing other methods have to be used [11, 7], in particular, the codimension of the crossing is of relevance.

The mathematical investigation of the time-dependent Born-Oppenheimer theory was initiated and carried out in great detail by Hagedorn. In his pioneering work [9] he constructs approximate solutions to (6) of the form ϕq⁡(t),p⁡(t)⊗χj​(q⁡(t))\phi_{q(t),p(t)}\otimes\chi_{j}(q(t)), where ϕq⁡(t),p⁡(t)\phi_{q(t),p(t)} is a coherent state carried along the classical flow, (q⁡(t),p⁡(t))=Φt​(q0,p0)(q(t),p(t))=\Phi^{t}(q_{0},p_{0}). The difference to the true solution with the same initial condition is of order ε\sqrt{\varepsilon} in the L2L^{2}-norm over times of order ε−1\varepsilon^{-1} in atomic units and the approximation holds until the first hitting time of ∂Λ×ℝn\partial\Lambda\times{\mathbb{R}}^{n}. In a recent work Hagedorn and Joye [10] construct solutions to (6) satisfying exponentially small error estimates. In Hagedorn’s approach the “adiabatic and semiclassical limits are being taken simultaneously, and they are coupled [10]”.

In our paper we carefully separate the space-adiabatic and the semiclassical limit. One immediate benefit is the generalization of the first order analysis of Hagedorn from coherent states to arbitrary wave functions.

Let us explain our result for the space-adiabatic part in more detail. We assume that there is some region Λ⊂ℝn\Lambda\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n} in the nucleonic configuration space, such that some subset σ∗​(X)\sigma_{*}(X) of σ​(He​(X))\sigma(H_{\rm e}(X)) is separated from the remainder of the spectrum by a gap for all X∈ΛX\in\Lambda, i.e.

dist⁡(σ∗​(X),σ⁡(He​(X))∖σ∗​(X))≥d>0for​all​X∈Λ.{\rm dist}\big(\sigma_{*}(X),\sigma(H_{\rm e}(X))\setminus\sigma_{*}(X)\big)\geq d>0\quad{\rm for\,\,all\,\,}X\in\Lambda\,.

Λ\Lambda could be punctured by small balls (for n=2n=2) because of band crossings. Λ\Lambda could also terminate because the point spectrum merges in the continuum, which physically means that the molecule loses an electron through ionization. Let P∗​(X)P_{*}(X) be the spectral projection of He​(X)H_{\rm e}(X) associated with σ∗​(X)\sigma_{*}(X) and P∗=∫Λ⊕d​X​P∗​(X)P_{*}=\int^{\oplus}_{\Lambda}\,dX\,P_{*}(X). We will establish that the unitary time evolution e−iHεt/εe^{-iH^{\varepsilon}t/\varepsilon} agrees on RanP∗P_{*} with the diagonal evolution e−iHdiagεt/εe^{-iH_{\rm diag}^{\varepsilon}t/\varepsilon} generated by Hdiagε:=P∗​Hε​P∗H_{\rm diag}^{\varepsilon}:=P_{*}H^{\varepsilon}P_{*} up to errors of order ε\varepsilon as long as the leaking through the boundary of Λ\Lambda is sufficiently small.

To complete the analysis one has to control the flow of the wave function through ∂Λ\partial\Lambda. One possibility is to simply avoid the problem by assuming that Λ=ℝn\Lambda={\mathbb{R}}^{n}, hence ∂Λ=∅\partial\Lambda=\emptyset. We will refer to this case as a globally isolated band. Of course, the set {(X,y)∈ℝn×ℝ:y∈σ∗​(X)}\{(X,y)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}\times{\mathbb{R}}:y\in\sigma_{*}(X)\} may contain arbitrary band crossings. As one of our main results, we prove that the subspace RanP∗P_{*} is adiabatically protected. In particular for the purpose of studying band crossings the full molecular Hamiltonian may be replaced by a simplified model with two bands only.

In general one has ∂Λ≠∅\partial\Lambda\not=\emptyset, to which we refer as a locally isolated band. To estimate the flow out of Λ\Lambda the only technique available seems to be semiclassical analysis. But this requires a control over the semiclassical evolution, for which one needs, at present, that {(X,y)∈Λ×ℝ:y∈σ∗​(X)}\{(X,y)\in\Lambda\times{\mathbb{R}}:y\in\sigma_{*}(X)\} contains no band crossings. Then {(X,y)∈Λ×ℝ:y∈σ∗(X)}=∪j{(X,y)∈Λ×ℝ:y=Ej(X)}\{(X,y)\in\Lambda\times{\mathbb{R}}:y\in\sigma_{*}(X)\}=\cup_{j}\,\{(X,y)\in\Lambda\times{\mathbb{R}}:y=E_{j}(X)\} is the disjoint union of possibly degenerate energy bands Ej​(X)E_{j}(X). We will prove that each band separately is adiabatically protected.

In the special case where σ∗​(X)=Ej​(X)\sigma_{*}(X)=E_{j}(X) is a nondegenerate eigenvalue for X∈ΛX\in\Lambda, e−iHdiagεt/εe^{-iH_{\rm diag}^{\varepsilon}t/\varepsilon} is well approximated through e−iHBOεt/εe^{-iH_{\rm BO}^{\varepsilon}t/\varepsilon} on L2​(ℝn)L^{2}({\mathbb{R}}^{n}). Since HBOεH_{\rm BO}^{\varepsilon} is a standard semiclassical operator, one can easily control the XX-support of the wave function and therefore prove a result for rather general Λ⊂ℝn\Lambda\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n}, for the details see Theorem 2. Roughly speaking, it says that if ϕt\phi_{t} is a solution of the effective Schrödinger equation for the nuclei

i​ε​∂ϕt∂t=HBOε​ϕt,i\varepsilon\frac{\partial\phi_{t}}{\partial t}=H^{\varepsilon}_{\rm BO}\phi_{t}\,, (8)

with suppϕ0⊂Λ\phi_{0}\subset\Lambda, then, modulo an error of order ε\varepsilon,

ψt:=ϕt​(X)​χj​(X,x)\psi_{t}:=\phi_{t}(X)\chi_{j}(X,x)

is a solution of the full Schrödinger equation (6) with initial condition ψ0​(X,x)=ϕ0​(X)​χj​(X,x)\psi_{0}(X,x)=\phi_{0}(X)\chi_{j}(X,x) as long as ϕt\phi_{t} is supported in Λ\Lambda up to L2L^{2}-mass of order ε\varepsilon. This maximal time span can be computed using the classical flow Φt\Phi^{t}.

As first observed by Mead and Truhlar [19], in general HBOεH_{\rm BO}^{\varepsilon} acquires as a first order correction an additional vector potential Ageo​(X)=−i⁡⟨χj​(X),∇Xχj​(X)⟩A_{\rm geo}(X)=-i\langle\chi_{j}(X),\nabla_{X}\chi_{j}(X)\rangle and (7) has to be replaced by

HBOε=ε2​12​(−i​∇X+Aext​(X)+Ageo​(X))2+Ej​(X).H^{\varepsilon}_{\rm BO}=\varepsilon^{2}\frac{1}{2}\Big(-i\nabla_{X}+A_{\rm ext}(X)+A_{\rm geo}(X)\Big)^{2}+E_{j}(X)\,. (9)

Multiplying χj​(X)\chi_{j}(X) with a smooth XX-dependent phase factor induces a gauge transformation for AgeoA_{\rm geo}, which implies that the physical predictions based on (9) do not change, as it should be. As noticed in [19], if Λ\Lambda is not contractible, then AgeoA_{\rm geo} cannot be removed through a gauge transformation and (9) and (7) describe different physics. Berry realized that geometric phases appear whenever the Hamiltonian has slowly changing parameters. Therefore Ageo​(X)A_{\rm geo}(X) is referred to as Berry connection, cf. [22] for an instructive collection of reprints. In fact, the motion of nuclei as governed by the Born-Oppenheimer Hamiltonian (9) is one of the paradigmatic examples for geometric phases.

If σ∗​(X)=E​(X)\sigma_{*}(X)=E(X) is kk-fold degenerate, not much of the above analysis changes. HBOεH_{\rm BO}^{\varepsilon} becomes matrix-valued and acts on L2​(ℝn)⊕kL^{2}({\mathbb{R}}^{n})^{\oplus k}, i.e.

HBOε=(ε22​(−i​∇X+Aext​(X))2+Ej​(X))​ 1k×k+ε2​((−i​ε​∇X)⋅Ageo​(X)+Ageo​(X)⋅(−i​ε​∇X)).H_{\rm BO}^{\varepsilon}=\left(\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{2}\Big(-i\nabla_{X}+A_{\rm ext}(X)\Big)^{2}+E_{j}(X)\right)\,{\bf 1}_{k\times k}+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\Big((-i\varepsilon\nabla_{X})\cdot A_{\rm geo}(X)+A_{\rm geo}(X)\cdot(-i\varepsilon\nabla_{X})\Big)\,.

The connection Ageo​(X)A_{\rm geo}(X) contains in general also off-diagonal terms and matrix-valued semiclassics must be applied. However, since the only nondiagonal term is in the subprincipal symbol, the leading order semiclassical analysis reduces to the scalar case and, in particular, agrees with the nondegenerate band case. We do not carry out the straightforward extension of Theorem 2 below to the degenerate band case, because the technicalities of matrix-valued semiclassics would obscure the simple ideas behind our analysis.

In their recent work [18] Martinez and Sordoni independently study the time-dependent Born-Oppenheimer approximation as based on techniques developed by Nenciu and Sordoni [20]. They consider the case of a globally isolated band for a Hamiltonian of the form (1) with smooth VV and Aext=0A_{\rm ext}=0. They succeed in proving the adiabatic decoupling to any order in ε\varepsilon for subspaces P∗εP_{*}^{\varepsilon} which are ε\varepsilon-close to the unperturbed subspaces P∗P_{*} considered by us. With this result, in principle, higher order corrections to the effective Hamiltonian (7) could be computed.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 contains the precise formulation of the results. Section 3 gives a short discussion of the semiclassical limit of HBOεH_{\rm BO}^{\varepsilon} and on how such results extend to the full molecular system. Proofs are provided in Section 4. In spirit they rely on techniques developed in [23] in the context of the semiclassical limit for dressed electron states. In practice the Born-Oppenheimer approximation requires several novel constructions, since the “perturbation” −ε22​Δ-\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{2}\Delta increases quadratically.

Our results can be formulated and proved in a more general framework dealing with, possibly time-dependent, perturbations of fibered operators. Also the gap condition can be removed by using arguments similar to those developed by Avron and Elgart in [1]. The general operator theoretical results will appear elsewhere [24].

This result should be understood as an adiabatic theorem for the subspaces RanP∗P_{*} and RanP∗⟂P_{*}^{\perp}, which are not spectral subspaces. Let us point out one immediate application of Theorem 2. The behavior near band crossings is usually investigated using simplified models involving only two energy bands and ignoring the rest of the spectrum, cf. [11, 7]. Theorem 2 shows that this strategy is indeed justified modulo errors of order ε\varepsilon.

(ii) Locally isolated bands

σ∗​(X)=E​(X)\sigma_{*}(X)=E(X) is a nondegenerate eigenvalue for all X∈ΛX\in\Lambda. Λ\Lambda may now be any open subset of ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} and for such a Λ\Lambda we assume H∞ and S. We also assume that Λ\Lambda is connected. Otherwise one could treat each connected component separately.

It is easy to see that, given H∞ and S, the family of projections P∗​(⋅)∈Cb∞​(Λ,ℒ⁡(ℋe))P_{*}(\cdot)\in C^{\infty}_{\rm b}(\Lambda,\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm e})). However, in order to “map” the dynamics from RanP∗P_{*} to L2​(Λ)L^{2}(\Lambda) we need in addition a smooth version χ⁡(⋅)∈Cb∞​(Λ,ℋe)\chi(\cdot)\in C^{\infty}_{\rm b}(\Lambda,\mathcal{H}_{\rm e}) of the normalized eigenvector of He​(X)H_{\rm e}(X) with eigenvalue E⁡(X)E(X). In other words we require the complex line bundle over Λ\Lambda defined by P∗P_{*} to be trivial. This always holds for contractible Λ\Lambda, but, as discussed below, also for some relevant examples where Λ\Lambda is not contractible.

Given a smooth version of χ⁡(X)\chi(X) with ‖χ⁡(X)‖=1\|\chi(X)\|=1, one has Re⟨χ⁡(X),∇Xχ​(X)⟩=0\langle\chi(X),\nabla_{X}\chi(X)\rangle=0, but, in general, Im⟨χ⁡(X),∇Xχ​(X)⟩≠0\langle\chi(X),\nabla_{X}\chi(X)\rangle\not=0. In the following we distinguish two cases: Either it is possible to achieve Im⟨χ~​(X),∇Xχ~​(X)⟩=0\langle\widetilde{\chi}(X),\nabla_{X}\widetilde{\chi}(X)\rangle=0 by a smooth gauge transformation χ⁡(X)→χ~​(X)=ei​θ​(X)​χ​(X)\chi(X)\to\widetilde{\chi}(X)=e^{i\theta(X)}\chi(X) or not. In the latter case

Ageo​(X):=−i⁡⟨χ⁡(X),∇Xχ​(X)⟩A_{\rm geo}(X):=-i\langle\chi(X),\nabla_{X}\chi(X)\rangle

is the gauge potential of a connection on the trivial complex line bundle over Λ\Lambda, the Berry connection, and has to be taken into account in the definition of the effective operator

HBOε:=ε22​(−i​∇X+Aext​(X)+Ageo​(X))2+E⁡(X)H_{\rm BO}^{\varepsilon}:=\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{2}\Big(-i\nabla_{X}+A_{\rm ext}(X)+A_{\rm geo}(X)\Big)^{2}+E(X) (14)

with domain W2​(ℝn)W^{2}({\mathbb{R}}^{n}). Thus AgeoA_{\rm geo} acts as an additional external magnetic vector potential. Although AextA_{\rm ext} and AgeoA_{\rm geo} appear in HBOεH_{\rm BO}^{\varepsilon} with an ε\varepsilon in front only, and therefore are not retained in the semiclassical limit to leading order, they do contribute to the solution of the Schrödinger equation for times of order ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}. If the full Hamiltonian is real in position representation, as it is the case for the Hamiltonians considered in the introduction whenever Aext=0A_{\rm ext}=0, then χ⁡(X)\chi(X) can be chosen real-valued. If, in addition, Λ\Lambda is contractible, the existence of a smooth version of χ⁡(X)\chi(X) with Im⟨χ⁡(X),∇Xχ​(X)⟩=0\langle\chi(X),\nabla_{X}\chi(X)\rangle=0 follows.

To define HBOεH_{\rm BO}^{\varepsilon} on L2​(ℝn)L^{2}({\mathbb{R}}^{n}) through (14), the functions E⁡(X)E(X) and Ageo​(X)A_{\rm geo}(X), which are a priori defined on Λ\Lambda only, must be continued to functions on ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n}. Hence we arbitrarily extend E⁡(X)E(X) and Ageo​(X)A_{\rm geo}(X) to functions in Cb∞​(ℝn)C^{\infty}_{\rm b}({\mathbb{R}}^{n}) by modifying them, if necessary, on Λ∖(Λ−δ/5)\Lambda\setminus(\Lambda-\delta/5) (cf. (17)) for some δ>0\delta>0. The parameter δ\delta will be fixed in the formulation of Theorem 2 and will appear in several places. It controls how close the states are allowed to come to ∂Λ\partial\Lambda.

The generic example for the Berry phase is a band crossings of codimension 2 (cf. [22, 11, 7]). If E⁡(X)E(X) is an isolated energy band except for a codimension 2 crossing, then Λ=ℝn∖{\Lambda={\mathbb{R}}^{n}\setminus\{closed neighborhood of the crossing}\} is no longer contractible, but the line bundle is still trivial. Although the underlying Hamiltonian is real, the Berry connection cannot be gauged away. Within the time-independent Born-Oppenheimer approximation Herrin and Howland [12] study a model with a nontrivial eigenvector bundle.

With the fixed choice for χ⁡(X)\chi(X) we have

Ran​P∗={∫Λ⊕d​X​ϕ​(X)​χ​(X);ϕ∈L2​(Λ)}⊂ℋ.{\rm Ran}\,P_{*}=\left\{\int_{\Lambda}^{\oplus}dX\,\phi(X)\chi(X);\,\phi\in L^{2}(\Lambda)\right\}\subset\mathcal{H}\,. (15)

Thus there is a natural identification 𝒰:\mathcal{U}: RanP∗→L2​(ℝn)P_{*}\to L^{2}({\mathbb{R}}^{n}) connecting the relevant subspace on which the full quantum evolution takes place and the Hilbert space L2​(ℝn)L^{2}({\mathbb{R}}^{n}) on which the effective Born-Oppenheimer evolution is defined. According to (15), we set

𝒰⁡(ϕ​χ)=ϕ,i.e.(𝒰​P∗​ψ)​(X)=⟨χ⁡(X),(P∗​ψ)​(X)⟩ℋe.\mathcal{U}(\phi\chi)=\phi\,,\qquad{\rm i.e.}\quad(\,\mathcal{U}P_{*}\,\psi\,)(X)=\langle\,\chi(X)\,,\,(P_{*}\,\psi)(X)\,\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\rm e}}\,.

Its adjoint 𝒰∗:L2​(ℝn)→\mathcal{U}^{*}:L^{2}({\mathbb{R}}^{n})\to RanP∗P_{*} is given by

𝒰∗​ϕ=∫Λ⊕d​X​ϕ​(X)​χ​(X).\mathcal{U}^{*}\phi=\int^{\oplus}_{\Lambda}\,dX\,\phi(X)\chi(X)\,.

Clearly 𝒰\mathcal{U} is an isometry and 𝒰∗​𝒰=𝟏\mathcal{U}^{*}\mathcal{U}=\bf 1 on RanP∗P_{*}. But 𝒰\mathcal{U} is not surjective and thus not unitary.

By construction, e−iHBOεt/εe^{-iH_{\rm BO}^{\varepsilon}{t/\varepsilon}} is a good approximation to the true dynamics only as long as the wave function of the nuclei is supported in Λ\Lambda modulo errors of order ε\varepsilon. Theorem 2 establishes that the electrons adiabatically follow the motion of the nuclei up to errors of order ε\varepsilon as long as the leaking through the boundary of Λ\Lambda is small. 3 Semiclassics for a single band

The semiclassical limit of Equation (8) with a Hamiltonian of the form (14) is well understood and there is a variety of different approaches. For example one can construct approximate solutions ϕq⁡(t)\phi_{q(t)} of (8) which are localized along a classical trajectory q⁡(t)q(t), i.e. along a solution of (16). Then it follows from Theorem 2 that ϕq⁡(t)​χ\phi_{q(t)}\chi is a solution of the full Schrödinger equation, (6), up to an error of order ε\varepsilon as long as q⁡(t)∈Λ−δq(t)\in\Lambda-\delta. Roughly speaking, this coincides with the result of Hagedorn [9]. In applications the assumption that the wave function of the nuclei is well described by a coherent state seems to be rather restrictive and a more general approach to the semiclassical analysis of a Schrödinger equation of the form (8) is to consider the distributions of semiclassical observables, i.e. of operators obtained as Weyl quantization aW,εa^{\rm W,\varepsilon} of classical phase space functions a:Z→ℝa:Z\to{\mathbb{R}}.

Consider a general initial wave function ϕε∈L2​(ℝn)\phi^{\varepsilon}\in L^{2}({\mathbb{R}}^{n}), such that ϕε\phi^{\varepsilon} corresponds to a probability measure ρcl​(d​q​d​p)\rho_{\rm cl}(dq\,dp) on phase space in the sense that for all semiclassical observables with symbols a∈Cb∞​(Z)a\in C^{\infty}_{\rm b}(Z)

limε→0|⟨ϕε,aW,ε​ϕε⟩−∫Za⁡(q,p)​ρcl​(d​q​𝑑p)|=0.\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\left|\langle\phi^{\varepsilon},\,a^{\rm W,\varepsilon}\,\phi^{\varepsilon}\rangle-\int_{Z}\,a(q,p)\,\rho_{\rm cl}(dq\,dp)\,\right|=0\,. (19)

The definition is equivalent to saying that the Wigner transform of ϕε\phi^{\varepsilon} converges to ρcl\rho_{\rm cl} weakly on test functions in Cb∞​(Z)C^{\infty}_{\rm b}(Z) [17]. An immediate application of Egorov’s theorem yields

uniformly on bounded intervals in time, where we recall that Φt\Phi^{t} is the flow generated by (16). In (20) one can of course shift the time evolution from the observables to the states on both sides and write instead

We mention some standard examples of initial wave functions ϕε\phi^{\varepsilon} of the nuclei which approximate certain classical distributions. In these examples one regains some control on the rate of convergence with respect to ε\varepsilon which was lost in (19).

(i) Wave packets tracking a classical trajectory.
